questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that "it's on a threat feed" is not, by itself, a reason to alert?
options: A single commercial feed can publish tens of thousands of IOCs a day, most low-confidence, stale, or irrelevant to your environment — piping all of it straight into detection teaches analysts to ignore threat-intel alerts within a week
Threat feeds are always generated by automated bots and contain no real intelligence
KQL cannot query against feed data without a watchlist already in place
STIX/TAXII feeds are technically incapable of including confidence scores
questions.explain: Unfiltered feed volume is the core alert-fatigue problem this chapter's scoring step exists to solve — most raw feed entries have nothing to do with your specific environment.

questions.q: What are the three signals this lesson combines into a single priority score?
options: Feed name, file size, and query latency
IOC type, source URL, and tag count
Confidence, relevance, and recency
CPU usage, network bandwidth, and disk space
questions.explain: Confidence (the feed's stated certainty), relevance (does it relate to your environment, including Lesson 14's "seen in environment" tag), and recency (how long ago it was reported) are the three inputs combined into priority_score().

questions.q: In the example priority_score() function, why are confidence and relevance each weighted at 0.4 while recency is weighted at only 0.2?
options: Because recency cannot be calculated in Python without an external API
Because weights are fixed by the STIX 2.1 specification and cannot be changed

Because an IOC confirmed to have touched your environment is still worth acting on even if its feed entry is a few weeks old, so the lesson leans harder on confidence and relevance than on how recently it was reported
Because confidence and relevance are always identical values, so splitting the weight between them is redundant
questions.explain: The weighting is a deliberate team judgment call, not an inherited default — this example prioritizes real corroboration (relevance) and source certainty (confidence) over pure freshness.

questions.q: What does tier_for_score() do with a raw priority score, and why does the lesson sort scored IOCs before assigning tiers?
options: It converts the score into a STIX pattern string for re-export to the original feed
It discards any IOC with a non-integer score before tiering
It deletes IOCs scoring below 50 permanently from the normalized list

It maps the score into a named bucket (auto_promote, analyst_review, archive) tied to a concrete next action; sorting first lets you also cap it to only the top N IOCs as a blunt noise control when a feed dumps an unusually large batch
questions.explain: Tiers turn a bare float into an actionable bucket, and sorting before tiering enables capping (e.g. "only the top 200") as an extra defense against a feed day with abnormal volume.

questions.q: According to this lesson, how should the 80/50 score thresholds used in tier_for_score() actually be tuned over time?
options: They should never change once set, regardless of outcomes

By tracking what happens to analyst_review IOCs after a human reviews them, and to auto_promote IOCs after they're acted on — adjusting the weighting or thresholds based on that real feedback, not guesses
By always doubling the thresholds every quarter
By asking the threat feed vendor to supply the correct thresholds
questions.explain: The 80/50 cutoffs are a starting point; the lesson explicitly calls for tuning based on real analyst feedback — if auto_promote IOCs are routinely wrong, or review IOCs are routinely dismissed, the thresholds or weights need to move.
